title: Riyadh Books Storage in Singapore as Tehran Sends Pezeshkian to Moscow's Gas Summit
subhead: Saudi Arabia signs a deal to park crude in Singapore's Jurong Rock Caverns from late 2027, the clearest admission yet that Gulf export routes cannot be assumed. The same weekend, Mecca pact envoys flew to Tehran and Iran's president headed to the GECF summit in Moscow to shop for energy-transit guarantees.

sections.heading: Aramco Goes Shopping for Tank Space It Does Not Have to Defend
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia has agreed with Singapore to store crude in the Jurong Rock Caverns, with deliveries beginning in the second half of 2027, Bloomberg reported on Oct. 26 and Oilprice.com confirmed via the Saudi and Singaporean energy ministries. The caverns hold 1.47 million cubic metres of crude and other liquids — roughly 9 million barrels. Aramco is looking for further storage abroad, per the same reporting.

Saudi energy minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman framed it as bringing supply closer to Asia: 'Bringing supply closer to the key Asian market would strengthen the flexibility of our supply network.' Singapore's energy minister Tan See Leng called it resilience against supply disruption.

The timing is the story. The deal was reported the day after Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure that included oil facilities, and after consecutive weekends of strikes on Aramco's Red Sea and Gulf assets. In practice Riyadh is conceding that it cannot guarantee the last leg of its own exports — so it is pre-positioning barrels east of Malacca, where neither Iran nor the Houthis can reach them.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first Gulf producer to buy strategic storage capacity overseas as a hedge against its own export corridors being cut. If it works, other Gulf NOCs follow — and the Gulf's role shifts from 'the source of the barrel' to 'one link in a supply chain that starts in Asia.'

sections.heading: The Mecca Pact Goes to Tehran, and Pezeshkian Goes to Moscow
sections.body:
On Monday, defense and intelligence chiefs from the three Mecca pact states — Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Turkish intelligence head Ibrahim Kalin — met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in Tehran, per AP and AFP reporting carried by CBS News. It was the first joint visit by the three since they formed their defense alliance in Mecca in August. Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei called the talks 'very good' and said a 'new atmosphere' was emerging; the meeting ended with an agreement to keep talking and no concrete announcement.

Two regional officials told AP that Yemen and Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia were on the agenda — which is the real subject, given the week Riyadh has had. A Qatari mediation team had been in Tehran the day before, coordinated with Washington.

Pezeshkian then flew to Moscow for the eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit, where the Kremlin said Putin will hold five bilateral meetings including with Pezeshkian and Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani (Interfax, via CBS). Pezeshkian's stated agenda: 'securing energy transit routes and eliminating insecurity in the Middle East,' which he attributed to the U.S.-Israeli assault on Iran that began Feb. 28.
sections.whyItMatters: Iran is now negotiating its security on two tracks at once — with Gulf Arab neighbors who are being bombed by its Houthi allies, and with the gas exporters' club in Moscow. The GECF summit gives Iran and Qatar a venue to talk transit guarantees without Washington in the room.

sections.heading: CENTCOM's 1.5 Billion Barrels Meets Kpler's 16.5 Million a Day
sections.body:
CENTCOM said on Oct. 25 that U.S. forces have helped Gulf partners export more than 1.5 billion barrels through Hormuz since summer, with 3,000-plus commercial vessels transiting under U.S. support in six months and 'over 95 percent' sailing safely, per Hürriyet Daily News. Admiral Brad Cooper, visiting troops in Hormuz, said primary transit routes 'remain free and clear of Iranian sea mines.'

Kpler data cited in the same report puts regional crude exports back at pre-war levels in September — at least 16.5 million barrels a day leaving the Gulf excluding Iran. Kuwait is pumping about 2 million b/d, down from 2.6 million pre-war, KPC chief Sheikh Nawaf Al-Sabah told Bloomberg on Oct. 5, after falling below 1 million b/d in the war's opening months.

Treat the two numbers differently. Barrels are moving; the cost and risk of moving them are not back to normal. That gap is what Riyadh's Singapore deal, Aramco's ship-to-ship transfers off Fujairah and Sohar, and Asia's halved U.S. crude orders are all responses to.
sections.whyItMatters: The Gulf is exporting at pre-war volumes but not at pre-war economics. Every fix — storage abroad, STS transfers, escorted convoys — adds a layer of cost and dependence on U.S. naval protection that did not exist a year ago.

sections.heading: India Starts Choosing the Gulf Again
sections.body:
BPCL, India's state refiner, expects Russian crude purchases to fall sharply in November, director of finance Vetsa Ramakrishna Gupta said after the company's Oct. 26 earnings. Russian crude was about 37% of BPCL's slate in July–September. The reason given is economics, not politics: freight costs have risen and Middle Eastern barrels are now cheaper delivered. The Russian premium over benchmark fell from $12–13 a barrel for October cargoes to $1–2 for December, per BPCL.

Reuters data cited in Indian coverage shows Middle Eastern crude hitting about 2.8 million b/d of India's imports in September — the highest since February 2026 — at roughly 54% of the total. Separately, Russian refiners are raising October diesel output after Moscow granted export quotas following the Trump-Putin supply deal, Reuters reported Oct. 26.

Meanwhile the first Russian diesel cargo under that deal, the Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes with about 300,000 barrels of ULSD from Primorsk, is due in New York on Nov. 7 — four days after the U.S. midterms. U.S. average diesel was $6.3172 a gallon on Oct. 23 versus $3.6315 a year earlier, per AAA.
sections.whyItMatters: Two trends are pulling in opposite directions: India is drifting back toward Gulf crude because freight makes Russian barrels uneconomic, while the U.S. is importing Russian diesel for the first time. The Russian discount is collapsing precisely because Moscow now has a sanctioned buyer in Washington.

sections.heading: Prices Fall on Diplomacy, Not on Supply
sections.body:
WTI retreated Monday from a five-month high of $103.28 to about $100.51, with Brent around $115, as traders weighed the Tehran talks against renewed escalation. TD Securities told FXStreet it expects crude 'skewed to the upside in the near term as escalation risk ahead of Israeli elections and U.S. midterm elections remains elevated,' adding that 'persistent tanker attacks by Iran appear to have been successful in reducing some Hormuz flows.' Danske Bank flagged the Fed, ECB and BoJ meetings Wednesday through Friday.

The pullback is a diplomacy trade, not a supply trade. Nothing in the physical market loosened this week: a vessel was reported on fire 63 nautical miles off Al-Faw in Iraq on Monday (UKMTO, 'suspicious activity'), a tanker was struck outbound in Hormuz on Friday (UKMTO, time-late report, crew safe), and the Saudi-led coalition shot down three more drones over Riyadh and a ballistic missile aimed at the capital.
sections.whyItMatters: With Israeli elections Tuesday and U.S. midterms on Nov. 3, the risk premium now trades on political calendars. That makes the market jumpy in both directions and makes any de-escalation signal — like Monday's Tehran meeting — temporarily worth more than it delivers.

sections.heading: Europe's Other Winter Problem: It Cannot Rebuild Its Industry
sections.body:
Bloomberg reported that the EU is preparing import restrictions on Chinese chemicals, furniture and machinery for early 2027, on top of a December cap on Chinese hybrid vehicles, as Brussels responds to deindustrialization-driven electoral losses. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has said the bloc will respond with 'some more safeguards.' The EU-China trade deficit stands at $404 billion.

The energy logic is uncomfortable. European gas storage was about 63% full in late August — the lowest for the season in nearly two decades — with TTF at its highest since 2023, as Qatari LNG stayed trapped behind Hormuz. ING's Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey warned the EU would struggle to hit even its flexible 75% target; Wood Mackenzie said 'Europe is approaching energy crisis territory.' TTF has since been quoted around €87–92/MWh.

Now Brussels is escalating a trade fight with the supplier of the rare earths and permanent magnets its remaining factories need to compete. As Zerohedge's write-up of Deutsche Bank's escalation-ladder analysis put it, the higher Brussels climbs, the greater the risk Beijing pulls those supplies.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe is fighting a trade war to protect industry it is simultaneously making uncompetitive with energy costs. If Beijing retaliates on critical materials, Brussels will have spent its leverage defending factories it cannot keep powered.

sections.heading: Asia Does Not Wait: Malaysia Reopens the Coal Question
sections.body:
Malaysia's Deputy Prime Minister Fadillah Yusof, who also holds the energy transition portfolio, said Monday at Singapore International Energy Week that the country may extend the operating life of existing coal units if reliability requires it — while keeping its pledge not to approve new coal plants. 'We are looking at all circumstances,' he said. 'At the end of the day, we have to make sure that we have power.'

The stated drivers, per Bloomberg's reporting, are the Middle East war's disruption of LNG exports and crude flows, plus a jump in electricity demand tied to Malaysia's data-centre buildout. Malaysia has diversified crude sourcing toward Africa since the war began, still targets 70% clean power by 2050, and plans for its last coal station to retire in 2044. Co-firing is under consideration if units stay online.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the second Southeast Asian government in a week to hedge its transition against fuel-security risk. Coal is becoming the region's default insurance policy against a Gulf it no longer trusts — a quiet, durable demand floor that no climate pledge changes.

bottomLine: Saudi Arabia's decision to rent 9 million barrels of underground storage in Singapore is the most honest thing any Gulf producer has said about this war: it is not buying back security, it is buying geography. The same weekend, Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish intelligence and defense chiefs flew to Tehran to talk about Houthi strikes, while Pezeshkian went the other direction to Moscow's GECF summit to bargain over gas transit. Prices fell Monday on the diplomacy headline, not on any physical loosening — Brent held near $115, WTI near $100, a tanker burned off Iraq and drones were shot down over Riyadh. The durable changes are quieter: India drifting back to Gulf crude as Russian freight gets expensive, Europe picking a trade fight with China while its factories freeze, and Malaysia keeping its coal plants as a backstop. The war is no longer only about who controls Hormuz. It is about who can put a barrel somewhere safe before it needs one.
sources: Bloomberg (via Oilprice.com, gCaptain), Reuters, CBS News/AP/AFP, Hürriyet Daily News/CENTCOM, Kpler, FXStreet (TD Securities, Danske Bank), Iran International, Lapaas Voice (BPCL earnings), Financial Express, Kommersant, AAA, UKMTO, Oilprice.com, Energy Risk IQ (TTF), Gas Infrastructure Europe/AGSI, ING (Patterson and Manthey), Wood Mackenzie, Oxford Institute for Energy Studies (Bill Farren-Price), Briefs Finance/Bloomberg (Malaysia), Zerohedge/Deutsche Bank (EU-China)
